faqs.q: Muscovy ducks have taken over our Tampa pond — what can be done?
faqs.a: Muscovy ducks are controlled under a federal Control Order: on your property, or by our crew with the property owner's permission, they may be captured and humanely euthanized without state or federal permits — but captured Muscovys may never be released elsewhere; relocation is flatly illegal for this species. We also cut the population's support: no feeding (the biggest driver), egg management where lawful, and hazing off docks and pools. Anyone offering to 'take the ducks to a farm' is offering an illegal release, and we will not do it.

Tampa.wildlife_intro:
Tampa is several cities in one for wildlife purposes: historic Ybor and Seminole Heights bungalows, South Tampa's waterfront streets, the university corridor, New Tampa's master plans, and industrial riverfront along the Hillsborough. Raccoons den in the old bungalow attics and the restaurant dumpsters of Ybor; roof rats own the palm-lined South Tampa blocks; bats roost in historic commercial buildings downtown; and along the river and in Town 'N Country's canals, iguanas — at their northern fringe here — appear as report-level sightings rather than established colonies.

South Tampa tile and historic Ybor woodwork demand two different crafts from the same truck, and our Tampa inspections are scheduled accordingly. Bat colonies in the older buildings are a specialty: identify the species, count exits at dusk, exclude only in the August 15 to April 15 window. Muscovy ducks in the retention ponds of every subdivision are handled under the federal Control Order — control on site is lawful, relocation never is. One call covers the whole city: (844) 544-3498.

faqs.q: Something is digging under my Brandon shed every night — what is it likely to be?
faqs.a: In Brandon the shortlist is skunk, opossum, and armadillo, and the sign separates them: a skunk leaves a neat dug entry and shallow grub holes in the lawn; an opossum's entry is messier with scattered debris; an armadillo digs many cone-shaped holes and a burrow that angles steeply. We confirm on inspection, trap the occupant, and skirt the shed with a buried apron — the step that separates a fix from a recurring subscription to the same problem.

faqs.q: We found a big burrow at our new Riverview lot line — can you clear it?
faqs.a: If it is a gopher tortoise burrow — a wide half-moon opening with a sandy apron, in open sunny ground — nobody can clear it without an FWC permit, and relocation is done only by an FWC Authorized Agent. Riverview's growth edges are full of tortoise burrows, and builders work around them by permit. If the burrow is an armadillo's — rounder, tighter, against a structure — we can trap and seal. The inspection exists to make exactly this call before anyone promises anything.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Plant City?
faqs.a: Plant City quotes are per-structure and practical: house, barn, and packing shed priced after one combined walk, in writing, with the food-storage fixes separated from the trapping so farm and household budgets each see their share.

faqs.q: Sandhill cranes are tearing up my Plant City lawn — what are my options?
faqs.a: Deterrence, patience, and never food. Florida sandhill cranes are State Threatened and protected; feeding one is illegal, and removal is not a service anyone may sell. Cranes grub for insects and sometimes peck screens during breeding season; motion-activated sprinklers, keeping pet food and seed inside, and letting a section of lawn be theirs usually ends the conflict. If a crane is injured or a pair nests in a construction zone, that is an FWC call — we will point you to it honestly.

Field-edge homes get the same tortoise-and-burrow literacy we teach everywhere in the sandy counties, because a strawberry field's neighbor is often a tortoise colony.

faqs.q: Why do squirrels love Temple Terrace attics so much?
faqs.a: Because the city is a squirrel highway system with houses attached. The attic entries are the same corners and vents as anywhere, but here the traffic never pauses, so sealing must be metal-backed and complete, with limbs cut back at least a squirrel's jump from the roof. Trapping without that seal, in this canopy, is a subscription, not a solution.

faqs.q: Roof rats are worse every winter in Apollo Beach — is that real?
faqs.a: It is a pattern we see across Tampa Bay's canal grids: cooler months push roof rats from the mangrove and palm fringe into the warm attics, and winter is also when seasonal fruit and unharvested citrus feed them best. The answer is permanent, not seasonal — seal the roofline once, cut palm-to-roof contact, and clear fallen fruit, and the winter wave breaks against a closed house. Trapping alone each winter is renting the same solution annually.

faqs.q: Otters are raiding my Lutz dock and fish — can they be removed?
faqs.a: River otters are native furbearers, and a visiting otter is usually passing along the lake's shoreline doing what otters do — a denning otter under a boathouse is a different matter and can be addressed under the nuisance rule with your authorization. Most dock complaints resolve with removing the attractants: no fish scraps at the cleaning table, secured bait, and a latched dock box. We will inspect, tell you honestly whether you have a resident or a tourist, and only sell removal when there is actually a resident to remove.

Lakeside living concentrates the calls: raccoons and otters around docks, roof rats in the lakefront homes, armadillos on the big lawns, and Muscovy ducks dominating community ponds. The Van Dyke corridor's growth keeps pushing new subdivisions against the greenbelt.

Lake lots get a shoreline-aware inspection in Lutz: boathouse gaps, dock boxes, and the low rooflines of Florida lake houses are the entries, with the attic second. Muscovy management follows the federal Control Order — on-property control lawful, release illegal — and we counsel associations through it plainly, because pond duck populations are usually a feeding problem wearing a duck costume.
